question.worked_solution:
Using the linearity property of double integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{6+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}(\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{R}\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-0){\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{6}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =3\cdot (-\frac{6}{y}{|}_{1}^{2}) \\  & =-18(\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A & =(2-1){\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{{3}^{3}}{3}-0 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\frac{6+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A=9+9=18.\end{aligned}
$$
